mainTopic: Welcoming שבת, a wood-chopper's liability for flying chips, and when an accidental killer is exempt from גלות because his act was שוגג קרוב למזיד.
overview: The amud opens with the end of a short אגדה about welcoming שבת like a bride and a queen, including רבי ינאי's custom of saying 'Come, bride.' Then a new משנה rules that someone chopping wood is liable when a chip causes damage, in every mix of public and private areas. The גמרא explains why all three cases had to be listed. A ברייתא follows about a carpenter whose flying chip kills a visitor. The carpenter is exempt if the visitor came in without permission and liable if he came in with permission. רבי יוסי בר חנינא says the carpenter pays four injury payments but is exempt from גלות. רבא first rejects the reason given for this and then explains it: the killing is שוגג קרוב למזיד, too careless for גלות. The גמרא tests this idea against the lasher who adds a lash and the man who throws a stone into a public area, and narrows each case until it is a plain accident. A second version places רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling on the visitor without permission. That leads to a challenge from a smith's sparks, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Going out to greet the bride, the queen
steps.stepSummary: The end of a quoted saying about welcoming שבת as a bride and queen, with a second version of the wording.
steps.simpleTranslation: 'Come, let us go out to greet the bride, the queen.' Some say the wording was: 'To greet שבת, the bride, the queen.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא is finishing an אגדה it began earlier about how sages eagerly went out to welcome שבת. It gives the saying and then a second version of its wording.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שבת is pictured as a royal bride whom we go out to meet. The second version simply names שבת directly, so it is clear who the 'bride and queen' is. This shows that hurrying toward שבת is a sign of honor.

keyTerms.meaning: To greet / toward, going out to meet someone

phrases.english: "Come and let us go out to greet the bride, the queen."
And some say it this way:
"To greet שבת, the bride, the queen."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Continues an אגדה about honoring שבת that began before this section.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: We go out to greet שבת as one greets a bride and a queen.

steps.title: רבי ינאי's custom of welcoming שבת
steps.stepSummary: רבי ינאי would wrap himself, stand, and call out 'Come, bride; come, bride.'
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי ינאי would wrap himself in his garment, stand, and say: 'Come, bride; come, bride.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a second sage's custom of welcoming שבת. This closes the אגדה before the new משנה starts.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי ינאי showed respect through his actions. He wrapped himself, as one dresses formally, and stood up as someone stands for an important guest. Then he greeted שבת directly as a bride.

keyTerms.meaning: Wraps himself (in a garment or טלית)

steps.whatToRemember: Welcoming שבת is like welcoming a royal bride. The sages dressed up, stood, and went out to greet her.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yannai would wrap himself and stand,
and say: "Come, bride; come, bride."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Adds another sage's practice of greeting שבת, parallel to the saying in step 1.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי ינאי honored שבת by wrapping himself, standing, and greeting it as a bride.

steps.title: Chopping wood that causes damage in another domain
steps.stepSummary: The new משנה rules that a wood-chopper is liable for damage from flying chips across three combinations of public and private areas.
steps.simpleTranslation: If someone chops wood in a public area and causes damage in a private area, or chops in a private area and causes damage in a public area, or chops in a private area and causes damage in someone else's private area, he is liable in all of these cases.
steps.whatsHappening: A new משנה begins. It lists three cases of chopping wood where a chip flies and causes damage, and says the chopper must pay in every one.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point is that it doesn't matter where he chopped or where the damage landed. In all three combinations of רשות הרבים and רשות היחיד he is חייב. The גמרא will next ask why so many cases had to be listed.

keyTerms.meaning: The public domain, an area everyone uses

steps.confusionAlert: Each case has two places: where he was chopping and where the damage happened. Read 'בִּרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד – וְהִזִּיק בִּרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים' as 'chopping in private, damage in public.'

phrases.english: MISHNAH:
One who chops wood in the public domain
and caused damage in private property;
in private property and caused damage in the public domain;
in private property
and caused damage in another person's private property,
he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A brand-new משנה, unrelated to the אגדה before it.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A wood-chopper whose chip causes damage is liable in every combination of public and private domains.

steps.title: Why the case of public-to-private was needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא explains that if the משנה had only taught the case of private-to-public, we would not know the public-to-private case.
steps.simpleTranslation: Both cases are necessary. If the משנה had only taught chopping in private and damaging in public, we would say he is liable there because many people are usually around in public. But from public into private, where crowds aren't usually present, we might say he is not liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts explaining why the משנה listed more than one case. This is the first half of the explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Damage in a public area might seem obviously his fault, because many people are always there and he should have expected someone to get hurt. In a private yard few people are around, so we might think he had no reason to expect damage. That is why the משנה had to teach the public-to-private case too.

keyTerms.meaning: Short for גְּמָרָא: the discussion of the משנה
And it is necessary (to teach each case)
For if it had taught (only this case)
I might say not (the law would be different)

phrases.english: GEMARA: And it is necessary;
phrases.notes: The גמרא means it was necessary for the משנה to list these cases separately.

phrases.english: for if it had taught only:
one who chops in private property
and caused damage in the public domain,
[he is liable] because crowds are common there;
but from the public domain to private property,
where crowds are not common,
I might say he is not liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains why the משנה in step 3 lists more than one case.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Without the public-to-private case, we might have exempted him there, since few people are present in a private area.

steps.title: Why the case of private-to-public was also needed
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא finishes its explanation: if the משנה had only taught public-to-private, we might exempt the reverse case, so both cases are needed.
steps.simpleTranslation: And if the משנה had only taught chopping in public and damaging in private, we would say he is liable because he was chopping in public without permission from the start. But from private into public, where he was chopping with permission, we might say he is not liable.
steps.whatsHappening: This is the second half of the 'it is necessary' explanation. It shows the other case also teaches something new, so both are needed.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Here the reasoning is about permission, not crowds. Someone chopping in a public area was doing something he had no right to do, so he is clearly at fault. Someone chopping in his own yard had every right to be there, so we might have exempted him. The משנה teaches that he is still liable.
steps.whyThisMatters: This shows that being on your own property doesn't excuse damage that flies onto others. It also shows that damage in a quiet private area still counts.

phrases.english: And if it had taught only:
from the public domain to private property,
[he is liable] because from the start he was acting without permission;
but from private property to the public domain,
where he is acting with permission,
I might say he is not liable.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְאִי תְּנָא: מֵרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים לִרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the two-sided explanation begun in step 4 by giving the reverse reasoning.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: Both the public-to-private and private-to-public cases are needed. Each blocks a different reason to exempt him (few people present, or acting with permission), and he is liable in both.

steps.title: Why the private-to-private case is also needed
steps.stepSummary: If the משנה had taught only the first two cases, we would have thought the private-to-private case is exempt. So the third case is needed too.
steps.simpleTranslation: If the משנה had taught only those two cases, I would say: in one he is liable because the public is often there, and in the other because he was working without permission. But from one private property to another private property, where the public is not often there and he was working with permission from the start, I might say he is not liable. So it is needed.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes its explanation of why the משנה listed all three cases. It shows that the third case, private to private, teaches something new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Each of the first two cases had its own reason for liability. In one, the chips land where people often walk. In the other, he was chopping in public, where he had no right to work. In the private-to-private case neither reason applies, so we might have exempted him, and the משנה teaches that he is still liable.

keyTerms.meaning: Many people are commonly found there
It is necessary (all the cases are needed)

steps.whatToRemember: All three cases in the משנה are needed. Each earlier case had a special reason for liability, and the private-to-private case shows he is liable even without those reasons.

phrases.english: And if it had taught only these two cases
this one is because many people are commonly there
phrases.notes: This is the case where chips fly from his property into the public area, where people walk.

phrases.english: and that one is because it was without permission
phrases.notes: This is the case where he was chopping in the public area, where he had no right to work.

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל מֵרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד לִרְשׁוּת הַיָּחִיד אַחֵר –
phrases.english: but from a private property to another private property
where many people are not commonly there
and from the start he was acting with permission
I might say he is not liable; so it is necessary.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Completes the צריכותא from steps 4-5 by explaining why the third case is needed
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: All three cases in the משנה are necessary. The private-to-private case shows liability even without crowds and without unauthorized activity.

steps.title: A carpenter's flying chip kills a visitor
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא rules that the carpenter is פטור if the visitor entered without permission and חייב if he entered with permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis taught: if someone enters a carpenter's shop without permission, and a wood chip flies off, hits him in the face, and he dies, the carpenter is exempt. If he entered with permission, the carpenter is liable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a new ברייתא on a related topic: a carpenter whose flying chip hurts someone in his shop.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The deciding factor here is whether the victim had permission to be in the shop. An uninvited intruder takes the risk on himself, but an invited guest does not, so the carpenter is responsible.

keyTerms.meaning: A chip or split piece of wood

phrases.english: The Rabbis taught:
one who enters the shop of a carpenter
without permission
and a wood chip flew off and struck him on his face
and he died: the carpenter is exempt.
But if he entered with permission, he is liable.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the משנה's wood-chopper cases to a related ברייתא about a carpenter's shop
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A carpenter is exempt if the victim entered without permission and liable if the victim entered with permission.

steps.title: What does 'liable' mean here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of liability the ברייתא means.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'liable' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a short clarifying question about the word 'liable' in the ברייתא. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Liability could mean money payments, or it could mean גלות for killing someone by accident. The גמרא wants to know which one the ברייתא means.

phrases.english: What is meant by 'liable'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the ruling in the ברייתא
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether 'liable' means money payments or גלות

steps.title: Four payments, but no exile
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי בר חנינא explains that the carpenter pays the four payments but is exempt from גלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: he is liable for four payments, but he is exempt from exile.
steps.whatsHappening: רבי יוסי בר חנינא answers the question: 'liable' means money payments, not גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ברייתא's 'liable' refers to the four payments of a person who injures another. Even though the carpenter is responsible, he does not go to an עיר מקלט.

keyTerms.meaning: The four payments for injuring someone
Exile to a city of refuge for accidental killing

steps.confusionAlert: Don't think 'liable' means the carpenter gets the full punishment for an accidental killing. He pays money but does not go into גלות.

phrases.english: Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina said:
He is liable for four things.
phrases.notes: These are the payments for the injury itself, pain, medical bills, and lost work time.

phrases.english: and he is exempt from exile,

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 8
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: Liable for the four payments, but exempt from גלות

steps.title: Why there is no exile: not like the forest
steps.stepSummary: The carpenter is not exiled because his case is unlike the forest case in the תורה, where both people are in a place they have a right to be.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is because the case is not similar to the forest. In a forest, this one enters his own area and that one enters his own area. But here, this one entered his fellow's property.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives the reason why the carpenter is exempt from גלות. It compares his case to the forest case in the תורה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The תורה's model for גלות is two people chopping wood in a forest, a place both have equal right to be. In the carpenter's shop, the victim came into someone else's private property, so the case does not match the תורה's model, and there is no גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: Forest (the תורה's model case for גלות)

steps.whyThisMatters: It shows that the rules of גלות follow the exact shape of the פסוק's forest case. Money liability can apply even when גלות does not.

phrases.english: because it is not similar to a forest.
In a forest, this one enters his own area,
and that one enters his own area;
but here, this one entered his fellow's property.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reason for the exemption from גלות stated in step 9
steps.mimraCoreRuling: גלות applies only where, as in the forest, both parties are in a place they may rightfully be. A victim who entered another's property does not fit this model.

steps.title: רבא's קל וחומר: the carpenter should be exiled even more
steps.stepSummary: רבא argues that the forest case points toward גלות for the carpenter, not away from it.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said: just the opposite, there is a קל וחומר. In the forest, each person went in on his own, without asking the other. Still, the victim is treated as if he came in with the killer's permission, and the killer goes to גלות. Here the victim came in with the carpenter's permission. Surely the carpenter should go to גלות!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא attacks the reason given in Step 10 for why the carpenter is not sent to גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 said the carpenter's case is weaker than the forest case, so no גלות. רבא turns this around. In the forest neither person had the other's permission, and there is still גלות. Here there was real permission, so the carpenter's case is stronger, and he should go to גלות all the more.

keyTerms.meaning: An argument from a lighter case to a stronger case ("all the more so")
Forest: the תורה's classic case of accidental killing
On his own decision, without asking anyone
He goes into exile, to an עיר מקלט

phrases.english: Rava said: On the contrary, it is a kal vachomer;
if in the case of a forest,
phrases.notes: This is the forest case in דברים 19:5.

phrases.aramaic: זֶה לְדַעְתּוֹ נִכְנָס וְזֶה לְדַעְתּוֹ נִכְנָס,
phrases.english: where this one entered on his own and that one entered on his own,

phrases.aramaic: נַעֲשָׂה כְּמִי שֶׁנִּכְנַס לְדַעַת חֲבֵירוֹ – וְגוֹלֶה;
phrases.english: he is treated like one who entered with the other's permission, and the killer is exiled;
this one, who entered with the other's permission,
is it not all the more so?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the reason in Step 10 for exempting the carpenter from גלות.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the carpenter is not exiled because his case is unlike the forest case.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Permission makes the case stronger than the forest case, so a קל וחומר requires גלות.

steps.title: Exile is not enough for him: שוגג קרוב למזיד
steps.stepSummary: רבא explains 'exempt from גלות' to mean that גלות is too light for him, because he was very careless.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רבא said: what does 'exempt from גלות' mean? It means גלות is not enough for him. This is the reason of רבי יוסי בר חנינא: the killing is accidental, but so careless that it is close to on purpose.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives a new explanation of רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling, now that the old reason has fallen.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The ruling stays the same: no גלות. The reason flips. He is not too innocent for גלות. He is too guilty, because he swung his tool when he knew a visitor was there. גלות only covers a simple accident, and his carelessness is beyond that.

keyTerms.meaning: Close to on purpose, very careless

steps.confusionAlert: 'Exempt from גלות' here does NOT mean he is let off easy. It means גלות is too small for how careless he was.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up a rule: a killing that is שוגג קרוב למזיד does not get גלות. The next steps test this rule.

phrases.english: Rather, Rava said:
What does 'exempt from exile' mean?
That exile is not enough for him.

phrases.aramaic: וְהַיְינוּ טַעְמָא דְּרַבִּי יוֹסֵי בַּר חֲנִינָא,
phrases.english: And this is the reason of Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina:

phrases.aramaic: מִשּׁוּם דְּהָוֵי לֵיהּ שׁוֹגֵג קָרוֹב לְמֵזִיד.
phrases.english: because it is an unintentional killing close to intentional.

steps.triggerLanguage: אֶלָּא אָמַר רָבָא: מַאי פָּטוּר מִגָּלוּת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers רבא's own קל וחומר by redefining what 'exempt from גלות' means.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The carpenter is exempt because his case is weaker than the forest case.
steps.terutzMaskana: He is exempt because his carelessness is so great that גלות cannot atone for it.

steps.title: Challenge from the lasher who added one lash
steps.stepSummary: רבא challenges his own idea: a lasher who adds one lash is sent to גלות, though that seems like שוגג קרוב למזיד.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא raised a challenge. A משנה says: if the lasher added one more lash and the man died, the lasher goes to גלות. But this seems to be שוגג קרוב למזיד, since he should have realized that people can die from one extra lash. Yet the משנה teaches that he goes to גלות!
steps.whatsHappening: רבא tests his new idea against a משנה that seems to go the other way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If שוגג קרוב למזיד means no גלות, then the lasher who gives an extra lash should not get גלות either, because he should have known it was dangerous. The משנה says he does get גלות. So either the rule is wrong, or this case is somehow different.

keyTerms.meaning: To bring to mind, to realize

phrases.aramaic: מֵתִיב רָבָא: הוֹסִיף לוֹ רְצוּעָה אַחַת,
phrases.english: Rava raised an objection: If he added one lash for him,
phrases.notes: This is from a משנה about lashes in court, where the court set how many lashes the man could take.

phrases.aramaic: וָמֵת – הֲרֵי זֶה גּוֹלֶה עַל יָדוֹ.
phrases.english: and he died, the lasher is exiled because of him.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא הָכָא דְּשׁוֹגֵג קָרוֹב לְמֵזִיד הוּא,
phrases.english: But here it is unintentional close to intentional,
since he should have realized
that people can die from one lash,
and yet it teaches: he is exiled!

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵתִיב רָבָא: הוֹסִיף לוֹ רְצוּעָה אַחַת
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Tests the rule from Step 12 against a משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that שוגג קרוב למזיד does not get גלות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The lasher's extra lash is also שוגג קרוב למזיד, yet the משנה sends him to גלות.

steps.title: רב שימי: the lasher miscounted
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי מנהרדעא answers that the lasher made an honest counting mistake, which is a plain accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שימי from נהרדעא said: the case is where he made a mistake in the counting.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי defends רבא's rule by explaining the lasher case differently.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the lasher simply lost count, he did not knowingly add a dangerous lash. That is an ordinary accident, not שוגג קרוב למזיד. So גלות fits, and רבא's rule still stands.

phrases.english: Rav Shimi from Neharde'a said:
It is where he erred in the counting.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שִׁימִי מִנְּהַרְדְּעָא: דְּטָעֵי בְּמִנְיָנָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in Step 13.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The lasher knowingly added a lash, which is שוגג קרוב למזיד.
steps.terutzMaskana: The lasher miscounted, which is a plain accident and gets גלות.

steps.title: רבא challenges it: the lasher doesn't do the counting
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects רב שימי's answer, because a judge counts the lashes, not the lasher.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא tapped him on his sandal and said to him: Does the lasher do the counting? But a ברייתא teaches: the greatest of the judges reads, the second one counts, and the third one says 'Strike him!'
steps.whatsHappening: רבא knocks down רב שימי's answer by showing who actually does the counting.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A judge counts the lashes. So the lasher could not have made a counting mistake himself. That reopens the challenge from Step 13, and the next step answers it.

keyTerms.meaning: Is that to say? (a surprised question)

steps.whatToRemember: רבא explained that the carpenter has no גלות because his act is שוגג קרוב למזיד, too careless for גלות. The lasher case challenges this, and the first 'miscounting' answer fails, since a judge does the counting. The next step gives רב שימי's revised answer.

phrases.english: Rava slapped him on his sandal,
phrases.notes: A way of showing he strongly disagreed with the answer.

phrases.english: and said to him: Is it he who counts?!
But it was taught: The greatest of the judges reads aloud,
phrases.notes: He reads פסוקים aloud while the lashes are given.

phrases.english: and the second counts,
and the third says: 'Strike him!'

steps.triggerLanguage: טְפַח לֵיהּ רָבָא בְּסַנְדָּלֵיהּ, אֲמַר לֵיהּ: אַטּוּ הוּא מָנֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רב שימי's answer from Step 14.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The miscounting explanation of the lasher case.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: According to the ברייתא, a judge counts the lashes, so the lasher cannot be the one who miscounted.

steps.title: רב שימי's new answer: the judge himself miscounted
steps.stepSummary: רב שימי מנהרדעא revises his answer: the lasher goes to גלות because the judge himself made the counting mistake, so the lasher was a plain accident.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, רב שימי מנהרדעא said: it is a case where the judge himself made the mistake.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שימי gives a new answer to replace the one רבא just rejected. Now the mistake belongs to the judge, not the lasher.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said the lasher cannot have miscounted, since the judge does the counting. So רב שימי says: fine, the judge himself counted wrong, and the lasher simply followed orders. That makes the lasher's killing a complete accident, not שוגג קרוב למזיד, so גלות fits him.

phrases.english: Rather, Rav Shimi of Neharde'a said:
It is where the judge himself erred.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the answer rejected in step 15 with a new case setup.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefining the case (who made the error)
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The lasher himself miscounted, which רבא showed is impossible since the judge counts.
steps.terutzMaskana: The judge miscounted; the lasher acted innocently, so his killing is a plain accident deserving גלות.

steps.title: Challenge from a stone thrown into a public area
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבא's idea: a משנה says someone who throws a stone into רשות הרבים and kills goes to גלות, though that seems like שוגג קרוב למזיד.
steps.simpleTranslation: They challenged: someone who throws a stone into a public area and kills goes to גלות. But here it is almost on purpose, since he should have realized that people are often found in a public area. And yet it teaches that he goes to גלות!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a source that seems to go against רבא's idea that very careless killers are too guilty for גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא said a killing that is close to on purpose does not get גלות. But throwing a stone into a busy public place is obviously risky, since people are always there. Still, the source says he goes to גלות, which seems to contradict רבא.

keyTerms.meaning: To bring to mind; to realize

phrases.aramaic: מֵיתִיבִי: הַזּוֹרֵק אֶת הָאֶבֶן לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים,
phrases.english: They raised an objection: One who throws a stone into the public domain,
and kills, he is exiled.

phrases.aramaic: וְהָא הָכָא, דְּשׁוֹגֵג קָרוֹב לְמֵזִיד הוּא –
phrases.english: But here, it is unintentional close to intentional,
since he should have brought it to mind
that in the public domain people are commonly found;
and it teaches: he is exiled!

steps.triggerLanguage: מֵיתִיבִי: הַזּוֹרֵק אֶת הָאֶבֶן לִרְשׁוּת הָרַבִּים
steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the lasher case is settled, a new source is brought against רבא's principle from step 12.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבא's principle that שוגג קרוב למזיד is too serious for גלות
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Throwing a stone into a busy public area is clearly very careless, yet the source gives גלות, so very careless killers do get גלות.

steps.title: Answer: he was knocking down his own wall
steps.stepSummary: רב שמואל בר יצחק answers that the case is someone tearing down his own wall, and the stones fell into the public area.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב שמואל בר יצחק said: it is a case where he is knocking down his wall.
steps.whatsHappening: רב שמואל בר יצחק defends רבא by changing how we picture the stone case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: He was not tossing stones into the street for no reason. He was doing normal work on his own wall, and stones fell out. That is much less careless, so it is a regular accident and fits גלות.

phrases.english: Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak said:
It is where he demolishes his wall.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב שְׁמוּאֵל בַּר יִצְחָק: בְּסוֹתֵר אֶת כּוֹתְלוֹ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 17.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The source speaks of someone carelessly throwing a stone into the street.
steps.terutzMaskana: The source speaks of someone demolishing his own wall, a normal activity, so it is a plain accident.

steps.title: But he should have looked first
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects: even when knocking down his wall, he should have checked whether people were below.
steps.simpleTranslation: He should have looked!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on רב שמואל בר יצחק's answer.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Knocking down a wall over a public area is still risky. A careful person would look first, so not looking still seems like שוגג קרוב למזיד.

phrases.english: He should have looked!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the answer of step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רב שמואל בר יצחק's wall case
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Even demolishing a wall requires checking for people below; failing to check is still very careless.

steps.title: Answer: he knocked it down at night
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא answers that he demolished the wall at night, when people are not usually around, so not checking was not very careless.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is where he demolishes it at night.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the last challenge by adding one more detail: it happened at night.
steps.deeperAnalysis: At night the street is normally empty, so it might seem reasonable for him not to expect anyone. That would make it a plain accident and keep רבא's principle intact. The next step challenges this answer.

phrases.english: Where he demolishes at night.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of step 19 by narrowing the case further.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: He demolished the wall in the daytime, when he should have checked.
steps.terutzMaskana: He demolished it at night, when no one is expected, so it is a plain accident deserving גלות.

steps.title: Even at night he should have looked
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the night-time answer: even at night, a person knocking down a wall should check whether anyone is below.
steps.simpleTranslation: Even at night he should have looked!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on the last answer from Step 20. Even at night, he should have checked before knocking the wall down.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 20 said that at night people are not around, so not checking is not very careless. The גמרא says that is not enough, because a responsible person checks even at night. If so, he should still count as careless, close to מזיד, and the case still does not fit a plain שוגג.

keyTerms.meaning: He should have; it was his duty to

phrases.english: At night too, he should have looked!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the night-time answer given in Step 20.
steps.kashyaTarget: The answer that he knocked the wall down at night.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Checking is expected even at night, so failing to check is still close to מזיד.

steps.title: He knocked the wall down by day into a garbage dump
steps.stepSummary: New answer: he knocked down his wall during the day, and the stones fell into a garbage dump.
steps.simpleTranslation: The case is where he knocks down his wall during the day, into a garbage dump.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new picture of the case. It happened in the daytime, and the stones fell into a garbage dump, a place where people are not usually found.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Instead of relying on the time of day, the answer relies on the place. A garbage dump is not a normal spot for people to be, so not checking there is not a big act of carelessness. That would make him a plain שוגג who goes to גלות.

phrases.english: Where he knocks down his wall during the day – into a garbage dump.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 21 by changing where the stones fell.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The case was at night, and even then he should have looked.
steps.terutzMaskana: The case is by day, into a dump where people are not normally present.

steps.title: What kind of garbage dump is this?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא sets up a dilemma. If people are often at the dump, he is close to מזיד. If they never are, he is אנוס. Either way, he should not go to גלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is this garbage dump like? If many people are commonly there, he acted deliberately! And if many people are not commonly there, he is a victim of circumstances beyond his control!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the garbage-dump answer with a two-sided question. Neither side seems to give a plain שוגג.
steps.deeperAnalysis: There are two options, and both fail. If people are often found there, throwing stones there is so careless that it counts as מזיד. If people are never found there, he could not have expected anyone, so he is אנוס and goes free. Either way, he does not fit the person who goes to גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case like? What are the exact circumstances?
Many people are commonly found there
Deliberate (or so careless it counts as deliberate)
Forced by circumstances; completely not at fault

steps.confusionAlert: Here מזיד does not mean he wanted to kill. It means he was so careless that he cannot be treated as an ordinary שוגג who goes to גלות.

phrases.english: This garbage dump, what is it like?
If many people are commonly there –
he acted deliberately!
And if many people are not commonly there –
he is a victim of circumstances beyond his control!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the garbage-dump answer of Step 22.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A dilemma: busy dump means מזיד, empty dump means אנוס. Neither is a plain שוגג who goes to גלות.

steps.title: רב פפא: a dump used at night, with only occasional daytime visitors
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא describes a middle case. The dump is used at night, not normally by day, but sometimes people do happen to sit there by day. So he is neither מזיד nor אנוס.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא said: It is needed only for a garbage dump that people use to relieve themselves at night but not during the day, though some people happen to come and sit there by day. He is not deliberate, since it is not used by day. He is also not a victim of circumstances, since some people do happen to come and sit there.
steps.whatsHappening: רב פפא escapes the dilemma by describing an in-between kind of dump. That makes the killer a true שוגג who goes to גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The dump is not normally used by day, so throwing stones there in the daytime is not so careless that it counts as מזיד. But people do sometimes happen to sit there by day, so he should have thought of it, and he is not completely אנוס. That middle ground is exactly a plain שוגג.

keyTerms.meaning: It is needed only for (a specific case)
Who happens to come by and sit

steps.whatToRemember: The stone-thrower in the משנה goes to גלות because the case is a middle case. People are not expected there, so he is not מזיד. But they sometimes come, so he is not אנוס. That is a true שוגג.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa said: It is needed only
for a garbage dump that people use to relieve themselves at night,
and do not use to relieve themselves during the day,
but there are some who happen to come and sit there;
he is not deliberate –
since people do not use it to relieve themselves during the day,
and he is not a victim of circumstances either –
since there are some who happen to come and sit there.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַב פָּפָּא לָא צְרִיכָא אֶלָּא בְּאַשְׁפָּה הָעֲשׂוּיָה לְהִפָּנוֹת בַּלַּיְלָה
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the dilemma of Step 23 with a middle-ground case.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the case to a middle situation between מזיד and אנוס
steps.terutzHavaAmina: A dump is either busy (מזיד) or empty (אנוס).
steps.terutzMaskana: A dump used at night, with only occasional daytime visitors, makes him a plain שוגג who goes to גלות.

steps.title: Second version: רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling refers to the first clause
steps.stepSummary: רב פפא reports in רבא's name that רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling, 'liable for four things and exempt from גלות', was said about the first clause: someone who entered the carpenter's shop without permission.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב פפא, in the name of רבא, taught it about the first clause. One who enters a carpenter's shop without permission, and a wood chip flies off, hits him in the face, and he dies: the carpenter is exempt. רבי יוסי בר חנינא said: He is liable for four things and exempt from גלות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a second version of how the earlier teaching was learned. In this version, רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling is attached to the ברייתא's first case, the visitor who came in without permission.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Until now, the discussion assumed רבי יוסי בר חנינא was talking about a later case in the ברייתא. Here רב פפא says in רבא's name that he was talking about the first case, where the visitor entered without permission. In that case רבי יוסי בר חנינא rules that the carpenter is exempt from גלות. If the visitor is only injured, the carpenter must pay four kinds of damage payments.

keyTerms.meaning: He taught it as referring to the first clause
Liable for four types of payment for injury

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a new argument against רב פפא's answer. It is a different version of where רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling belongs in the ברייתא.

phrases.english: Rav Pappa, in the name of Rava,
taught it as referring to the first clause:
phrases.notes: 'It' is רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling about the carpenter, which comes at the end of this step.

phrases.english: One who enters a carpenter's shop
without permission,
and a wood chip flew off at him
and struck him in his face,
and he died – he is exempt.
Rabbi Yosei bar Ḥanina said:
He is liable for four things,
phrases.notes: This is about a case where the visitor was injured and lived. Then the carpenter pays four kinds of injury payments.

phrases.english: and exempt from exile.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב פָּפָּא מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּרָבָא מַתְנִי לַהּ אַרֵישָׁא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a second version of the earlier teaching, placing רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling on the ברייתא's first clause.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In this version, רבי יוסי בר חנינא rules about one who entered the carpenter's shop without permission. The carpenter pays four injury payments if the visitor is hurt, and is exempt from גלות if the visitor dies.

steps.title: What the two versions mean for the 'with permission' case
steps.stepSummary: If רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling was said on the last clause, it applies even more to the first clause. If it was said only on the first clause, then in the last clause the killer goes to גלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whoever teaches the ruling on the last clause (entered with permission) would certainly apply it to the first clause (entered without permission). But whoever teaches it on the first clause holds that in the last clause, since the victim entered with permission, the carpenter is liable to גלות.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא spells out the practical difference between the two ways of teaching רבי יוסי בר חנינא's ruling.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If even a visitor who came in with permission does not send the carpenter to גלות, then a visitor who came in without permission certainly does not. But under the version from step 25, the ruling covers only the trespasser. A visitor who came in with permission is someone the carpenter should have watched out for, so the carpenter goes to גלות.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who teaches it (this version of the ruling)

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the next challenge: is someone really sent to גלות just because the victim entered with permission?

phrases.english: The one who teaches it on the last clause,
phrases.notes: The last clause is the case where the visitor entered with permission.

phrases.english: all the more so on the first clause;
and the one who teaches it on the first clause,
but on the last clause,
since it was with permission,
he is liable to exile.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Works out what follows from רב פפא's report of the version that places the ruling on the first clause.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Under the first-clause version, a carpenter whose visitor entered with permission and was killed goes to גלות.

steps.title: Challenge from the smith's sparks
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says a smith whose sparks killed a visitor is exempt even if the visitor entered with permission. That seems to contradict the idea that permission makes him liable to גלות.
steps.simpleTranslation: But is he really liable to גלות? A ברייתא teaches: if someone enters a smith's workshop and sparks fly off, strike him in the face, and he dies, the smith is exempt, even if the visitor entered with permission!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the view from step 26 that entering with permission makes the killer liable to גלות.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 26 said that permission to enter means the owner should have been careful, so he goes to גלות. This ברייתא says outright that the smith is exempt even when the visitor entered with permission. The two rulings seem to clash.

keyTerms.meaning: But is it really so? (opens a challenge)

phrases.english: But is he liable to exile?
But isn't it taught:
One who enters a smith's workshop,
and sparks flew off
and struck him on his face and he died,
he is exempt,
phrases.notes: The smith is the one who is exempt here, meaning he does not go to גלות.

phrases.english: and even if he entered with permission!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the conclusion of step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that entering with permission makes the killer liable to גלות.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A ברייתא exempts the smith even when the victim entered with permission.

steps.title: The ברייתא is about the smith's apprentice
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא is talking about the smith's apprentice, not an ordinary visitor.
steps.simpleTranslation: What case is the ברייתא dealing with? With the smith's apprentice.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by narrowing the ברייתא to one specific kind of person.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the 'permission' in the ברייתא belongs to an apprentice who works there, the ruling might not apply to an ordinary guest. Then it would not contradict step 26.

keyTerms.meaning: What case are we dealing with here? (used to narrow a source)

phrases.english: Here, what are we dealing with?
With the smiths' apprentice.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 27.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case of the ברייתא
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא covers any visitor who entered with permission.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא covers only the smith's apprentice.

steps.title: May an apprentice be killed?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the smith would be exempt for killing his apprentice. The apprentice is not someone who deserves less care.
steps.simpleTranslation: Does the smiths' apprentice stand to be killed?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 28.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An apprentice has every right to be in the workshop. If anything, the smith should watch out for him even more. So calling him an apprentice does not explain why the smith is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: Does he stand to be killed? (does he deserve to be harmed carelessly?)

phrases.english: The smiths' apprentice,
does he stand to be killed?
phrases.notes: He means: is the apprentice someone the smith is allowed to be careless about?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 28.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the ברייתא is about the apprentice.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Being an apprentice gives no reason for the smith to be less careful.

steps.title: The master told him to leave
steps.stepSummary: The case is where the smith keeps urging the apprentice to leave, and the apprentice refuses.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a case where his master keeps urging him to leave, and he does not leave.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds a detail to the apprentice case to explain why the smith is exempt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The apprentice stayed against his master's clear wishes. That shifts some of the responsibility onto the apprentice himself.

phrases.english: When his master urges him to leave,
and he does not leave.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 29.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding a detail to the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: An apprentice in the workshop is someone the smith must watch out for.
steps.terutzMaskana: This apprentice refused his master's order to leave.

steps.title: Refusing to leave does not justify killing him
steps.stepSummary: Even if the apprentice refused to leave, the smith still knows he is there and should be careful.
steps.simpleTranslation: And just because his master urged him to leave, does he now stand to be killed?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the answer from step 30.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An apprentice who disobeys is still a person standing in the room. As long as the smith knows he is there, he should hold off working or be careful. So disobeying alone does not explain the exemption.

phrases.english: And because his master urges him to leave,
does he stand to be killed?!

steps.triggerLanguage: וּמִשּׁוּם דְּרַבּוֹ מְסַרְהֵב בּוֹ לָצֵאת לְמִיקְטְלֵיהּ קָאֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 30.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that the apprentice's refusal to leave exempts the smith.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The smith knows the apprentice is still there, so he should be careful.

steps.title: The smith thought he had left
steps.stepSummary: The smith believed the apprentice had already gone out when the sparks flew.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is where the smith thought he had left.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא adds one more detail: the smith did not know the apprentice was still there.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since the smith reasonably believed the room was empty, he had no reason to be careful. That is why he is exempt.

keyTerms.meaning: When he thought the other person had left

phrases.english: When he thought he had left.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 31.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Adding a detail to the case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The smith knew the apprentice was still in the workshop.
steps.terutzMaskana: The smith believed the apprentice had already left.

steps.title: Then why mention an apprentice at all?
steps.stepSummary: If the reason is that the smith thought the person had left, the same would be true of any other person. So why limit the ברייתא to an apprentice?
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, then any other person too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges step 32. The answer comes on the next amud.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The exemption now rests only on the smith thinking the room was empty. That reason works for any visitor, not just an apprentice. So the apprentice detail from step 28 no longer seems needed, and the challenge from step 27 comes back.
steps.confusionAlert: This is a question, not a conclusion. The גמרא is not ruling that any visitor is exempt. It is pointing out that the apprentice explanation has lost its point.

phrases.english: If so,
another person also!
phrases.notes: He means: any other visitor who the smith thought had left would also make the smith exempt.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the answer of step 32 by showing it makes the apprentice detail pointless.
steps.kashyaTarget: Explaining the ברייתא as specifically about an apprentice.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: If the smith is exempt because he thought the person had left, the same applies to any person, so the apprentice detail adds nothing.
